title: Operations and Supply Chain Management
tagline: Make processes, stock and suppliers work, with hands-on practice in every module
summary: Learn the foundations of operations and supply chain management: processes and bottlenecks, inventory and demand forecasting, quality and continuous improvement, suppliers and logistics, improvement proposals and key performance indicators. Every module has a hands-on lab.

modules.title: Operations foundations
modules.summary: What operations management is, how processes work and how to find waste and bottlenecks.
modules.outcome: You can describe the input-process-output view, map a process, spot waste and find the bottleneck.
modules.intro: Every organisation, from a street stall to a hospital to a bank, turns inputs into outputs that customers value. Operations management is the discipline of doing that efficiently, reliably and safely.

topics.title: Inputs, processes and outputs
topics.html:
Examples
BusinessInputsProcessOutput
BakeryFlour, eggs, ovens, bakersMixing, baking, decoratingCakes delivered on time
HospitalPatients, doctors, equipment, medicineDiagnosis, treatmentRecovery and care
Online shopStock, website, pickers, couriersOrder, pick, pack, deliverParcels at the door

The four most common measures of operations performance are cost, quality, speed and flexibility. Improving one often costs another, so management means choosing the balance that customers value.

Performance objectives
ObjectiveQuestion
CostHow much does it cost to produce and deliver?
QualityDoes it meet customers' expectations without errors?
SpeedHow quickly can the customer get it?
DependabilityDo we deliver when promised?
FlexibilityCan we change what, when and how much?

Check what you just learned

1. Which is an input to a bakery?
  • A delivered cake
  • Flour and ovens (correct)
  • A happy customer
  • A review

Resources go in.
keyPoints: Operations transforms inputs into outputs customers value.
Balance cost, quality, speed, dependability and flexibility.

topics.title: Process mapping and waste
topics.html:
A process map shows each step in order. Even a simple drawing on paper reveals delays, loops and steps that nobody remembers adding.

The eight wastes (a common lean list)
WasteMeaningExample
DefectsErrors that need reworkWrong message on a cake
OverproductionMaking more than is neededFifty unordered cakes
WaitingIdle timeWaiting for the oven
Non-used talentNot using people's skills and ideasIgnoring staff suggestions
TransportUnneeded movement of itemsMoving boxes twice
InventoryToo much stockIngredients expiring
MotionUnneeded movement of peopleWalking to far shelves
Extra processingMore work than the customer valuesOver-decorating a plain order

Mapping steps

  1. Choose the process and its start and end.
  2. List the steps in order as they really happen, not as they should.
  3. Add time for each step and waiting between steps.
  4. Mark which steps add value for the customer.
  5. Circle the longest wait or slowest step.
Tip

Walk the process yourself. The place where it really happens differs from the manual.

When you map a process, record two kinds of time for each step: the time someone is actually working (touch time) and the time the item waits before the next step. In most offices and workshops, the waiting time is far larger than the working time. A tailoring order might need only six hours of real work but take five days because it sits in queues. Reducing the waiting, by smoothing the flow, limiting how much work is started at once and clearing blockers, often shortens delivery times much more than making people work faster.

It is also worth asking customers directly what they value. A bakery might assume that customers value elaborate decoration, when most care mainly about taste, freshness and arriving on time. Knowing this changes which steps count as value-adding and which as extra processing. Where customers value something, protect and improve it; where they do not, find ways to simplify or remove the step without harming safety or quality.

Check what you just learned

1. Making more than customers ordered is:
  • Transport
  • Motion
  • Overproduction (correct)
  • Quality

A classic waste.
keyPoints: Map the real process, time each step and mark value-adding steps.
Know the eight wastes.

topics.title: Bottlenecks and capacity
topics.html:
Definition

Bottleneck. The step in a process with the lowest capacity. It sets the output of the whole process: a chain moves at the speed of its slowest link.

Formula · Capacity of a step

capacity per hour = (60 / minutes per unit) × number of workers or machines

Decorating takes 10 minutes per cake with 1 decorator: 60 / 10 × 1 = 6 cakes per hour.

Find the bottleneck

Change the times and workers at each step and see the system's capacity and output per day.

Adjust Mixing minutes per cake, Baking minutes per cake, Ovens, Decorating minutes per cake, Decorators and see Mixing capacity per hour, Baking capacity per hour, Decorating capacity per hour change.

Managing a bottleneck

  • Never let it idle: keep it fed and running.
  • Do not spend money speeding up non-bottleneck steps.
  • Move simple tasks away from the bottleneck.
  • Add capacity there if the demand justifies it.
  • Re-check: another step becomes the new bottleneck.

Check what you just learned

1. To raise the output of a process you should first improve:
  • Any step
  • The first step
  • The fastest step
  • The bottleneck (correct)

It sets the pace.

Key terms: flip and sort

Process
A series of steps that transform inputs to outputs
Bottleneck
The step with the lowest capacity
Waste
Activity that does not add customer value
Capacity
Maximum output over a period
Lean
An approach focused on value and waste reduction
keyPoints: The bottleneck sets the output.
Improve the bottleneck, not the other steps.

practical.intro: Pick a simple process, such as making tea or processing a library return.

modules.title: Inventory and demand
modules.summary: Forecast demand, decide how much to order and keep the right amount of stock.
modules.outcome: You can classify stock with ABC analysis, calculate economic order quantity, forecast demand and set a reorder point.
modules.intro: Too little stock loses sales; too much ties up cash and spoils. Inventory management is the art of keeping just enough.

topics.title: Why hold stock, and what it costs
topics.html:
Reasons to hold stock
ReasonExample
Meet demand during lead timeSelling while waiting for the next delivery
Smooth uneven demandBuilding stock before a festival
Get quantity discountsBuying a full truckload
Protect against uncertainty (safety stock)A late delivery or an unexpected rush
Costs of stock
CostMeaning
OrderingCost of placing and receiving an order
HoldingStorage, insurance, spoilage, capital tied up (often 15 to 30% of value a year)
Stock-outLost sales, rushed deliveries and unhappy customers

Order often and you pay a lot in ordering costs but keep little stock. Order rarely and you save on orders but hold more. The best order quantity balances the two.

Common mistakes

  • Ordering only when someone notices stock is low.
  • Counting only purchase price, not holding cost.
  • Treating all items the same.

Check what you just learned

1. Holding costs include:
  • Storage and spoilage (correct)
  • Customer smiles
  • Marketing
  • Free space

Keeping stock is not free.
keyPoints: Stock protects service but costs money.
Balance ordering cost and holding cost.

topics.title: ABC analysis and EOQ
topics.html:
ABC classes
ClassShare of itemsShare of valueControl
AAbout 10 to 20%About 70 to 80%Tight: frequent review, accurate counts
BAbout 30%About 15 to 20%Moderate
CAbout 50%About 5%Simple: bulk ordering, low attention
Formula · Economic order quantity (EOQ)

EOQ = √(2 × annual demand × cost per order / holding cost per unit per year)

√(2 × 2,400 × 300 / 12) = √120,000, about 346 units.

EOQ explorer

Change demand and costs to see the best order size.

Adjust Annual demand (units), Cost per order (rupees), Holding cost per unit per year and see EOQ (units), Orders per year, Total yearly ordering plus holding cost change.

EOQ assumes steady demand and fixed costs, so treat it as a guide. Round to practical pack sizes and adjust for minimums and shelf life.

Check what you just learned

1. Class A items are:
  • Many and low in value
  • Few and high in value (correct)
  • All the same
  • Never ordered

They deserve the most control.
keyPoints: ABC focuses effort on the few high-value items.
EOQ balances ordering and holding costs.

topics.title: Forecasting and reorder points
topics.html:
Simple forecasting methods
MethodHowGood for
NaiveNext period equals last periodStable demand
Moving averageAverage of the last n periodsSmoothing noise
SeasonalUse the same period last year, adjustedFestivals, weather
JudgementExpert knowledge of promotions or eventsNew products, special cases
Formula · Reorder point

reorder point = demand during lead time + safety stock

If you sell 120 units a week and the lead time is 2 weeks, lead-time demand is 240. Add safety stock for uncertainty.

Formula · Safety stock (simple form)

safety stock = z × standard deviation of demand during lead time

z is about 1.65 for a 95% chance of not running out.

Good practice

  • Keep records of actual sales and compare them to forecasts.
  • Treat forecasts as ranges, not exact numbers.
  • Update forecasts regularly.
  • Share forecasts with suppliers.
  • Use judgement for events your history does not show.
Watch out

Forecasts are always wrong by some amount. Judge a forecast by how useful it is for decisions and how its error compares with alternatives.

Check what you just learned

1. Reorder point equals:
  • Annual demand
  • Safety stock only
  • Lead-time demand plus safety stock (correct)
  • EOQ

Order when stock reaches it.

Key terms: flip and sort

Lead time
Time between ordering and receiving
EOQ
Economic order quantity
Safety stock
Extra stock for uncertainty
Reorder point
Stock level that triggers an order
Stock-out
Running out of stock
keyPoints: Moving averages smooth demand; reorder point = lead-time demand + safety stock.
Forecasts are ranges that need review.

modules.title: Quality and continuous improvement
modules.summary: Measure quality, find root causes and improve in small steps.
modules.outcome: You can use basic quality tools, calculate defect rates, interpret simple control limits and run an improvement cycle.
modules.intro: Quality is not an inspection at the end; it is built into every step. The tools in this module help you find what goes wrong, why and how to prevent it.

topics.title: What quality means
topics.html:
Views of quality
ViewMeaning
Fitness for purposeDoes it do what the customer needs?
Conformance to specificationDoes it match the design?
ConsistencyIs it the same every time?
Service qualityIs the experience reliable, responsive and courteous?
Formula · Defect rate

defect rate = defects / items checked

10 defects in 500 items is 2%.

Formula · Cost of poor quality

cost = defects × (cost to fix or replace + damage to reputation)

Rework, returns, scrap, extra inspection and lost customers all count.

Preventing defects is usually cheaper than finding them, and finding them early is cheaper than finding them at the customer.

Tip

Count defects by type, not just in total. The type tells you what to fix.

Check what you just learned

1. Defect rate for 10 defects in 500 items is:
  • 0.2%
  • 50%
  • 20%
  • 2% (correct)

Divide 10 defects by 500 items to get 2%.
keyPoints: Quality means fitness for purpose and consistency.
Prevent and detect defects early; count them by type.

topics.title: Basic quality tools
topics.html:
Tools
ToolUse
ChecklistMake sure steps are not missed
Pareto chartRank causes by count to find the vital few
Fishbone (cause-and-effect)Organise possible causes by category
FlowchartShow process steps
Run / control chartPlot results over time to spot trends and unusual points
HistogramShow the spread of results

The Pareto idea is that a few causes produce most problems. Here, the top three causes account for 76% of the 500 complaints. Fixing those yields most of the benefit.

Using a fishbone

  • Write the problem at the head.
  • Draw main branches: people, methods, machines, materials, measurement, environment.
  • Brainstorm causes under each.
  • Select likely causes and test them with data.

Check what you just learned

1. A Pareto chart ranks causes by:
  • Count or cost (correct)
  • Alphabet
  • Age
  • Colour

Largest first.
keyPoints: Pareto finds the vital few; fishbone organises causes; control charts show drift.
Test suspected causes with data.

topics.title: Control limits and improvement cycles
topics.html:
All processes vary. A control chart shows the average and limits (often the average plus or minus three standard deviations). A point outside the limits, or a run of points on one side of the average, signals that something has changed and is worth investigating.

Common cause and special cause
TypeMeaningResponse
Common causeNatural variation always presentImprove the whole system
Special causeA specific event: new supplier, broken tool, new operatorFind and fix or learn from the cause
Worked example

A control example

A factory's daily defect rate averages 2% with a standard deviation of 0.5%. On Friday the rate is 6%.

  1. The upper limit is 2% + 3 × 0.5% = 3.5%.
  2. 6% is well above it: a special cause.
  3. Investigate: what changed on Friday? A new batch of material? A different operator?

Answer. Control charts tell you when to look, and when not to overreact.

Watch out

Do not react to every small fluctuation. Changing a stable process because of normal variation often makes it worse.

Check what you just learned

1. A point far outside the control limits suggests:
  • Normal variation
  • A special cause worth investigating (correct)
  • A perfect process
  • Nothing

Something changed.

Key terms: flip and sort

Defect rate
Defects divided by items checked
Pareto
A few causes cause most effects
Control chart
A chart of results over time with limits
PDCA
Plan, do, check, act
Special cause
A specific, identifiable reason for variation
keyPoints: Control limits separate normal variation from special causes.
Use PDCA: plan, do, check, act.

modules.title: Logistics, sourcing and supply chain
modules.summary: Choose suppliers, move goods and manage supply chain risk.
modules.outcome: You can compare suppliers by total cost, describe the main logistics choices and plan responses to supply risks.
modules.intro: A supply chain is the network of organisations that turn raw materials into products in the customer's hands. Decisions about suppliers, transport and stock can matter as much as the product itself.

topics.title: The supply chain and its flows
topics.html:
Three flows
FlowDirectionExample
GoodsForward (and back for returns)Flour from mill to bakery
InformationBoth waysOrders, forecasts, delivery updates
MoneyBackwardPayments to suppliers

The 'bullwhip effect' describes how small changes in customer demand can cause bigger and bigger swings in orders as you move upstream. Each link adds a safety margin, and the result is too much stock at times and shortages at others. Sharing real demand information helps to reduce it.

Key questions

  • Who are our critical suppliers and customers?
  • How long does each link take?
  • Where is the stock?
  • What happens if one link fails?

Check what you just learned

1. The bullwhip effect describes:
  • Faster delivery
  • A type of whip
  • Amplified swings in orders upstream (correct)
  • Lower costs

Information distortion.
keyPoints: Goods, information and money flow through a chain.
Share demand information to reduce the bullwhip effect.

topics.title: Choosing and managing suppliers
topics.html:
Total cost of ownership
ElementExample
Purchase price95 rupees per unit
Transport and handling12,000 per shipment
Duties and taxes5,000
Quality costsDefects, returns, rework
Delay and risk costsLate delivery, stock-outs
Payment terms30 days credit has a value
Formula · Cost per usable unit

total cost / (units × (1 − defect rate))

Cheap supplies with high defects or delivery trouble may cost more in the end.

Selecting suppliers

  1. Define what you need: quality, quantity, time, price.
  2. Collect quotes and references.
  3. Visit or audit key suppliers.
  4. Check their finances, capacity and ethics.
  5. Start with small orders.
  6. Review performance: on-time delivery, quality, responsiveness.
Watch out

Check suppliers for safe working conditions, fair labour and legal compliance. Poor practices in your supply chain are your risk and your responsibility.

Check what you just learned

1. Total cost of ownership includes:
  • Price only
  • Only payment terms
  • Only duties
  • Price plus transport, quality, delay and other costs (correct)

Count all costs.
keyPoints: Compare total cost of ownership, not only price.
Review supplier performance and ethics.

topics.title: Transport, warehousing and resilience
topics.html:
Transport modes
ModeStrengthWeakness
RoadFlexible, door to doorCostly for long distances, traffic
RailCheap for bulkFixed routes, less flexible
SeaCheapest for long distanceSlow
AirFastExpensive
Digital deliveryInstant for downloadsNot for physical goods

Warehouse basics

  • Store fast-moving items closest to dispatch.
  • Label locations and keep records accurate.
  • First in, first out for items that spoil.
  • Count regularly (cycle counting).
  • Keep it safe and clean.
Making the chain resilient
StrategyIdea
Diversify suppliersAvoid a single point of failure
Buffer stock for critical itemsTime to react
Source nearerShorter, less exposed chain
VisibilityTrack orders and shipments in real time
Plan for disruptionHave a written response plan
Tip

Ask for each critical item: if this supplier disappeared next week, what would we do?

Check what you just learned

1. Cheapest mode for bulk over long distances is usually:
  • Sea or rail (correct)
  • Air
  • Courier
  • Bicycle

Slow but economical.

Key terms: flip and sort

Supply chain
The network from raw materials to customer
Bullwhip effect
Amplified swings in orders upstream
Total cost of ownership
All costs of acquiring and using a product
Lead time
Time from order to delivery
Resilience
Ability to cope with disruption
keyPoints: Choose transport mode by cost, speed and flexibility.
Build resilience with diversity, buffers and visibility.

modules.title: Operations in practice
modules.summary: Combine tools to propose improvements, work with people and consider safety and sustainability.
modules.outcome: You can write an improvement proposal with costs and benefits, involve people in change and consider safety and environmental impact.
modules.intro: Tools alone do not improve operations; people do. This module covers making the case for change, bringing people with you and doing so safely and sustainably.

topics.title: Making the case for change
topics.html:
An improvement proposal
SectionContent
Problem and evidenceWhat is wrong, with numbers
Proposed changeWhat you will do
Cost and benefitInvestment, saving and payback
RisksWhat could go wrong; responses
Next stepsOwners and dates
Formula · Payback period

payback = investment / yearly saving

60,000 / 90,000 = 0.67 years, about 8 months.

Persuading with evidence

  1. Measure before you change.
  2. Start with a pilot.
  3. Show results in a simple chart.
  4. Quote money, time and safety in the same terms leaders use.
  5. Acknowledge risks honestly.
Tip

A one-page proposal with three numbers (problem size, cost, payback) is often more persuasive than twenty pages.

Check what you just learned

1. A payback of 0.67 years means:
  • Six years
  • Eight months (correct)
  • One week
  • Never

0.67 × 12 months.
keyPoints: Show the problem, change, cost, benefit, risk and next steps.
Payback = investment / yearly saving.

topics.title: People, change and safety
topics.html:
Operations improvements succeed or fail on whether the people doing the work support them. Those who do the job know the problems best and often have the best ideas.

Bringing people along

  • Explain why the change is needed.
  • Involve operators in the design and the pilot.
  • Train properly.
  • Listen to concerns and respond.
  • Share results and credit the team.
Basic safety principles
PrinciplePractice
Hierarchy of controlsEliminate the hazard, substitute, use engineering controls, then administrative controls, then protective equipment
Report near-missesTreat them as free lessons
Training and supervisionPeople must know how to work safely
HousekeepingClear walkways, labelled storage
Stop-work authorityAnyone may stop unsafe work
Watch out

Never trade safety for speed or cost. Follow the laws and standards that apply where you operate, and involve qualified safety professionals.

Check what you just learned

1. The best protection against a hazard is to:
  • Wear protective equipment only
  • Ignore it
  • Eliminate it where possible (correct)
  • Train after an accident

Eliminate first.
keyPoints: Involve the people doing the work.
Safety is never traded for speed or cost.

topics.title: Sustainability and responsibility
topics.html:
Operations use materials, energy and water, and create waste and emissions. Good operations reduce these because they save money and protect communities and the environment.

Sustainable operations ideas
IdeaExample
Reduce wasteCutting layouts that reduce scrap
Reuse and recycleReturn crates and recycled packaging
Save energyEfficient machines, switching off idle equipment
Smarter transportCombine deliveries, plan routes
Responsible sourcingChoose suppliers with fair labour and environmental practices

Waste reduction saving

Change the annual material spend and the waste rates to see the yearly saving and payback.

Adjust Annual material spend (rupees), Current waste (percent), Target waste (percent), Cost of the change (rupees) and see Yearly saving (rupees), Payback in years change.

Good habits

  • Measure waste, energy and water.
  • Set targets and share progress.
  • Include sustainability in supplier checks.
  • Be honest in claims; avoid exaggerated green marketing.

Check what you just learned

1. Reducing waste usually:
  • Has no effect
  • Costs more always
  • Harms quality always
  • Saves money and resources (correct)

Often a double win.

Key terms: flip and sort

Payback
Time to recover an investment
Pilot
A small trial of a change
Near-miss
An incident that could have caused harm
Hierarchy of controls
A ranking of ways to manage hazards
Circular economy
Keeping materials in use
keyPoints: Reducing waste and energy saves money and protects the environment.
Measure and report honestly.

options: Better than relying on protective equipment

modules.title: Tools, data and next steps
modules.summary: Use spreadsheets and simple data for operations decisions, and plan your next steps.
modules.outcome: You can build a basic operations dashboard in a spreadsheet and describe the career paths and tools in the field.
modules.intro: Most operations decisions can be made with a spreadsheet and clear thinking. This final module shows how to set up simple indicators and where to go next.

topics.title: Key performance indicators
topics.html:
Common KPIs
AreaKPIFormula
DeliveryOn-time delivery rateorders on time / total orders
QualityDefect ratedefects / items checked
InventoryStock turnoverannual cost of goods sold / average stock value
CostCost per unittotal cost / units produced
ProductivityUnits per labour hourunits / hours worked
ServiceOrder fill rateorders filled complete / total orders

Good KPIs

  1. Few: four to six that matter.
  2. Clearly defined and measured the same way.
  3. Shown with targets.
  4. Reviewed regularly with action owners.
  5. Balanced: do not chase cost at the expense of quality.
Tip

Make one-page dashboards. If a chart does not trigger a decision, remove it.

Every KPI should have an owner who can influence it and a target that is realistic but demanding. A number that nobody owns is only decoration. It also helps to show the trend over several weeks and not just this week's value, because a single bad day is rarely as informative as a pattern. When a KPI moves in the wrong direction, ask first whether the measurement changed, then whether the process changed, and only then who is responsible.

Check what you just learned

1. On-time delivery rate is:
  • Orders on time / total orders (correct)
  • Orders / days
  • Cost / orders
  • Defects / orders

A simple ratio.
keyPoints: Choose a few clear KPIs with targets.
Balance cost, quality, speed and service.

topics.title: Spreadsheets for operations
topics.html:
Handy functions
TaskFunction
Add upSUM
AverageAVERAGE
Largest and smallestMAX, MIN
Count matchingCOUNTIF
Total matchingSUMIF
DecideIF, AND
VariationSTDEV
Square rootSQRT
Round up to whole unitsROUNDUP

Good spreadsheet habits

  • Put inputs in labelled cells and refer to them, not typed numbers.
  • Lock fixed cells with dollar signs.
  • Check totals against another source.
  • Colour inputs differently from formulas.
  • Keep a clean copy of the original data.

Common mistakes

  • Typing numbers into formulas so they cannot be updated.
  • Mixing units, such as hours and minutes.
  • Not checking the result against a quick mental estimate.

Check what you just learned

1. Why refer to input cells in formulas?
  • It looks neat
  • So you can update values and see the result (correct)
  • It is faster to type
  • It hides errors

Flexibility and fewer mistakes.
keyPoints: Use labelled inputs and a few key functions.
Check results against a rough estimate.

topics.title: Where this leads
topics.html:
Roles in the field
RoleTypical work
Operations analystData, KPIs, process improvement
Supply chain plannerDemand forecasts, inventory, orders
Logistics coordinatorTransport, warehouse, delivery
Procurement officerSourcing and supplier management
Quality assistantInspection, audits, improvement
Operations managerRunning a site or service

Building your profile

  • Do a small improvement project and measure the result.
  • Learn spreadsheets well, then a data or planning tool.
  • Learn the basics of accounting and costing.
  • Build communication and teamwork skills.
  • Consider recognised professional courses and certifications offered by established bodies if you want formal credentials.

This course gives a practical foundation. It is not an accredited qualification, but the skills are the same ones employers look for in entry-level operations roles.

Tip

Keep a log of improvements with before-and-after numbers. It is a powerful story in an interview.

Check what you just learned

1. What is a strong way to show your skill?
  • Claiming to be good
  • Silence
  • A small improvement project with before-and-after numbers (correct)
  • A long list of terms

Evidence beats claims.

Key terms: flip and sort

KPI
Key performance indicator
Stock turnover
How often stock is sold and replaced
Fill rate
Share of orders filled complete
Dashboard
A one-page view of KPIs
Procurement
Buying goods and services
keyPoints: Operations offers many roles; build evidence with small projects.
Spreadsheets, costing and communication are core skills.
